 Nov 19, 2026 4 Student Loan Moves That Could Save You $10K or More
 You've got a wealth of options, but they all change your obligations. Written by Stephanie Mickelson | Edited by Brendan McGinley Add us as a preferred source Student loan payments can weigh down even the savviest budgeters, especially if you’re working with a tight income or have unexpected circumstances come up that strain your finances. If you need some more wiggle room in your monthly budget , there are ways to reduce your monthly student loan payments, and the right one depends on your individual circumstances.
 A caveat: One general rule that comes with lowering payments is that it could extend the length of your repayment term and result in paying more for your loans overall.

 Jack Wang, a college financial aid advisor and host of the Smart College Buyer podcast, said borrowers should ask themselves if the lower payment is worth the extra interest or longer repayment term. It's important to consider how it will impact your finances in the future as well. 
 “If a borrower refinances to lower a monthly payment or goes on an income-driven repayment plan, it doesn’t have to be a permanent choice,” Wang said. Borrowers have the option to refinance later or pay off the loan early when they have more money. 
 July 1, 2026 marked several changes to the federal government’s student loan programs, especially for those who were enrolled in the SAVE repayment plan that went into effect in 2023. As of now, these are a few of the options available that could potentially save you $10,000 or more each year.
 Income-Driven Repayment Plan
 An income-driven repayment plan (IDR), including the Income-Based Repayment Plan (IBR) and Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP), uses a percentage or your adjusted gross income to determine your monthly payments. 
 Wang said this plan offers an overlooked benefit in the form of tax strategies. 
 “Payments on an IDR are based on adjusted gross income,” he said, “so anything that can be done to lower AGI helps.” 
 Some options he included are changing your tax filing status or maximizing pre-tax deductions like retirement account or HSA contributions. 
 Refinancing Through a Private Education Loan Lender
 “When you refinance your loan through a private education loan lender, it allows a borrower to extend the loan term, reducing monthly payments,” said Tom O’Hare, founder of Get College Going and Senior Partner with Pivotal College Years. 
 You can refinance both private loans and federal loans. Refinancing may also allow you to get a better interest rate which can lower monthly payments and ultimately reduce the total payback amount. 
 Consolidating Federal Loans
 If you have federal student loans, you can consolidate them into one loan that uses a weighted average of the loan interest rates to set the new rate. When you consolidate federal loans, you’re still eligible for federal loan benefits, like an IDR and potential loan forgiveness. You may also be able to extend the repayment term, but while this will reduce monthly payments now, it can result in paying more in interest over the life of the loan. 
 Contact Your Loan Servicer
 O’Hare recommends that borrowers in need of financial assistance and payment relief should contact their loan servicer.
 Certain options like forbearance, interest-only payments or a short-term payment reduction may be available. Your loan servicer can work with you to understand your circumstances and speak specifically to your loan and the current federal loan program options and requirements.
